title: Runtime LTS Channel — Proposal Draft (Release Eng)
content:
Owner: Connor O’Brien (Release Eng)
PM: Talia Benson
Exec sponsor: Mateo Alvarez (Runtime)
Last updated: 2025-02-03
Status: Draft proposal for ADR approval

Summary
We should introduce a Long Term Support (LTS) channel for the Redwood serving runtime to serve Dedicated and Private customers who need a stable baseline for 6–12+ months. The LTS line will prioritize kernel + scheduling stability, predictable patch cadence, and audited/reproducible artifacts over rapid feature delivery. The main output is a branch strategy, a backport rubric and approvals workflow, a patch cadence with clear expectations, and packaging support (Private installer + Helm pinning) to make upgrades/rollbacks safe.

Why now (customer pain + business impact)
We have increasing enterprise pressure for “change control” around runtime upgrades. Several accounts are asking for:
- A stable runtime baseline they can validate once and then keep for an extended period.
- Predictable patch cadence that aligns with their internal CAB/change windows.
- A formal backport policy so they can trust that patches contain only security and critical fixes.
- Verifiable artifacts (checksums/signing) and mapping to commits for audit.

Observed pain points (from Support/CS + deals in flight)
1) Forced upgrades due to incidents/regressions
   - Customers hit latency regressions or correctness issues after moving to a new minor runtime (example: post-1.18 upgrade regressions). They want to “pin” a known-good runtime line while still receiving critical fixes.

2) Performance variance is treated as a production incident
   - Enterprise platform teams are extremely sensitive to P95 latency and throughput swings, especially on Dedicated capacity. They prefer stable scheduling/attention kernel behavior even if it means slower adoption of new heuristics.

3) Private deployments need audit + reproducibility
   - Private customers are asking for checksums, signing, and artifact provenance (who built it, what commit, what dependencies). They also want rollback guidance that works with their installer/Helm.

4) Support/Engineering escalation churn
   - Without an LTS line, critical customer bugs often trigger urgent upgrade requests to “whatever is latest,” which increases operational risk for customers and increases load on our on-call + support escalation path.

Goals
- Provide an enterprise-friendly “slower-change” runtime channel with:
  - Defined support window (target: 6–12 months per LTS line; details below).
  - Predictable patch cadence (target: monthly; with out-of-band security patches).
  - Explicit backport policy (what qualifies; risk rubric; required tests/perf gates; approvals).
  - Reproducible, auditable artifacts (checksums/signing; provenance; optional SBOM).
  - Release notes suitable for enterprise change management.

Non-goals
- Not a forked architecture: LTS remains close to mainline.
- Not guaranteeing feature parity with mainline.
- Not promising that every bugfix will be backported—only security + critical/severe issues meeting the rubric.

Proposed customer promise (draft)
1) Support window
- Each LTS line is supported for 12 months from initial LTS branch cut (preferred) OR 9 months minimum (fallback if maintenance cost is too high).
- We will publish an end-of-support date up front.
- We will provide at least one “overlap period” where two LTS lines are supported concurrently (e.g., 2–3 months overlap) to allow customers to plan migrations.

2) Patch cadence
- Regular patch cadence: monthly patch releases (e.g., runtime 1.18.1-lts, 1.18.2-lts, …).
- Security patches: out-of-band as needed. Target SLA: 72 hours for confirmed critical vulnerabilities with customer impact; otherwise next patch window.
- Emergency hotfix process with tightened approvals and explicit communication.

3) Backport policy (high-level)
Eligible changes (draft tiers):
- Security fixes (CVE or internal security advisory) impacting runtime components or dependencies included in LTS artifacts.
- Sev1 correctness/availability issues (crash, data corruption, request loss, major functional break) with customer reproduction and clear fix.
- Sev2 performance regressions with verified degradation against defined baselines (e.g., sustained p95 regression above threshold on canonical workloads).

Generally not eligible:
- Feature work, refactors, “nice to have” optimizations.
- Behavior changes with unclear blast radius.
- Changes that require large diffs or touch multiple subsystems unless the risk is explicitly accepted.

Risk rubric (draft)
Each backport candidate gets a risk score (Low/Medium/High) based on:
- Diff size and subsystem surface area (kernel, scheduler, caching, routing, etc.).
- Test coverage quality (new regression test included? deterministic?).
- Performance impact risk (hot path? GPU kernel change? scheduling heuristics?).
- Operational complexity (config changes, upgrade steps, new dependencies).

Approval workflow (draft)
- Release Eng (Connor) + Runtime owner for affected area (Hiro for kernels; Sofia for scheduling; Noah for architecture) + SRE sign-off (Sean/Rafael) for any High-risk or perf-related backports.
- For emergency security patches: Security sponsor sign-off (Dr. Aisha Rahman / Hanae Suzuki) + SRE + Release Eng required.

What LTS means in practice (scope and guarantees)
- The LTS channel is a “stability contract” for kernel + scheduling behavior.
- We will freeze certain defaults (e.g., autotune parameters and experimental batching heuristics) to reduce surprise variance. Customers can override via config flags if needed, but the default behavior stays stable within an LTS line.
- We will publish a compatibility matrix per patch (GPU SKUs covered by perf gates; minimum driver/toolchain requirements; known issues).

Branching / versioning (needs ADR)
Options under consideration:
A) Dedicated LTS release branches
- Example: runtime-1.18-lts branch created from the 1.18.x line at a chosen “golden” commit.
- Patch tags: 1.18.1-lts, 1.18.2-lts, etc.
Pros: Clear separation of LTS changes; straightforward cherry-picks; aligns with enterprise expectations.
Cons: Ongoing maintenance burden; CI/build divergence risk.

B) Tags only (no separate branch)
- Keep mainline; tag LTS builds off of specific commits.
Pros: Minimal branch management.
Cons: Harder to enforce “slower-change” contract; backports become messy; customers perceive instability.

Recommendation (draft): Option A, with strict policy to keep LTS close to mainline and minimize divergence.

Packaging and distribution requirements (Hosted/Dedicated/Private)
Hosted API
- LTS is less of a customer-facing “pin” unless product chooses to expose it, but internally we should use LTS for a subset of enterprise traffic where stability is the priority.
- Need monitoring and roll-forward/rollback playbooks.

Dedicated
- Customers should be able to select an LTS line and optionally pin to a specific patch.
- Patch rollout should support canary, A/B, and fast rollback.

Private
- Must support explicit pinning to an LTS patch image/tag.
- Must provide:
  - Artifact checksums (and ideally signatures).
  - Release notes URLs and version metadata.
  - Rollback instructions that are tested.
- Helm + installer support needs to be first-class (no manual image surgery for customers).

CI / performance gating (draft)
We need stricter gates than mainline for LTS patches:
- Deterministic build + reproducible artifact generation.
- Mandatory scheduler smoke tests for typical regression patterns: mixed prompt lengths, overload, backpressure, load shedding.
- Performance gates on canonical workloads across a minimum GPU SKU set:
  - Measure p50/p95 latency and throughput; compare to established LTS baseline.
  - Thresholds (placeholder):
    - p95 latency regression <= 3% on tier-1 workloads, <= 5% on tier-2.
    - Throughput regression <= 3% (unless explicitly accepted with customer-facing note).
  - Waiver process: rerun to rule out flake; require SRE + Runtime approval to ship with waiver.

Release notes expectations (draft)
Enterprise-grade “slower-change” notes, per patch:
- Executive summary (what matters; whether patch is recommended/mandatory).
- Categorized changes: Security / Reliability / Performance / Compatibility / Tooling.
- Upgrade notes (anything operators must do).
- Known issues + workarounds.
- Compatibility matrix:
  - Supported GPU SKUs for perf gates
  - Supported driver/toolchain ranges (as applicable)
  - Notes on quantization profiles and kernel defaults
- Artifact verification section (checksums/signing; provenance pointers).

Ownership and operational model (draft)
- Release Eng owns the mechanics: branch health, release calendar, tag discipline, artifact publication, release notes generation.
- Runtime owns correctness/perf for LTS backports; subsystem leads accountable for risk assessment.
- SRE owns rollout monitoring, SLO dashboards for LTS traffic, and escalation path.
- Support/CS owns intake and triage; requires an explicit backport request template.

Escalation / “mandatory patch” criteria (draft)
A patch is “mandatory” if:
- It fixes a critical security issue affecting production deployments.
- It fixes a Sev1 crash/data corruption issue with active customer impact.
- It resolves a severe performance regression verified in customer environment and in our perf suite.
Otherwise patches are “recommended” with guidance on who should upgrade.

Success metrics (draft)
- Fewer incident-driven upgrades for enterprise accounts (Support + CS qualitative + count of urgent upgrade escalations).
- Reduced time-to-ship for critical fixes to enterprise customers without requiring a minor/major upgrade.
- Stable P95 variance within LTS lines (tracked via perf gates + production SLO dashboards).
- Improved enterprise security posture: artifact provenance available for every patch; ability to answer “what changed?” quickly.
- Deal enablement: LTS not a blocker for regulated prospects (track via Sales/CS notes).

Proposed timeline (draft)
Phase 1 (2–3 weeks)
- Gather requirements from Runtime, SRE, Product, Support/CS.
- Decide branching/versioning scheme via ADR.
- Draft backport rubric + approvals workflow.
- Draft release notes template.

Phase 2 (4–6 weeks)
- Implement CI and perf gates for release branches.
- Build/release automation for cherry-picks/backports.
- Add artifact signing/checksums and provenance metadata.
- Private installer + Helm pinning support.

Phase 3 (4 weeks)
- Pilot with 1–3 enterprise accounts.
- Cut first patch; validate gates and comms.
- Iterate on runbooks and tooling.

Phase 4 (GA)
- Publish docs + internal training (Support/CS/Sales).
- Establish steady-state cadence; monthly reporting.

Open questions (need decisions / input)
1) Support window length
- 12 months vs 9 months vs 6 months. What is realistic given expected patch volume and staffing?

2) How many concurrent LTS lines?
- One active line only vs overlap (two lines concurrently). Overlap is better for customers but increases cost.

3) What counts as Sev2 performance regression for LTS eligibility?
- Define thresholds and required evidence (perf-canary + customer env logs + reproducible benchmark).

4) Toolchain and dependency policy
- Do we allow toolchain bumps in LTS (CUDA/driver/toolchain) for security reasons? If so, how do we communicate and gate it?

5) Kernel default freeze scope
- Exactly which knobs are frozen to ensure predictable performance? (autotune defaults, batching heuristics, scheduler tuning)

6) Artifact signing
- What is the minimum viable signing story for Private enterprise customers (cosign? GPG? internal KMS)? Who holds keys and what is the access model?

7) Release notes ownership and workflow
- Who curates the human summary? (proposal: Release Eng drafts; Runtime signs off; Product reviews for customer-facing clarity)

8) Customer visibility
- Does Console expose an “LTS channel” selector by default for Dedicated? For Private, what is the UX in docs/installer values?

9) Backport conflict handling
- What’s our policy when a fix is non-trivial to cherry-pick (requires refactor or dependency changes)? Do we reject, re-implement minimally, or accept divergence?

10) CI capacity for perf gates
- Need dedicated benchmark runners to avoid blocking. Who owns provisioning and how do we schedule around patch week?

Next steps (proposal)
- Schedule 60-min ADR decision meeting: Connor + Mateo + Noah + Hiro + Sofia + Sean + Marissa.
- Draft ADR: branching/versioning + support window + concurrent line policy.
- Define initial LTS candidate version (tentative: 1.18 line).
- Build minimal “backport request template” with Support (Dev Patel) and CS (Rachel Kim).

Notes / context references
- Support tickets motivating LTS: SUP-18421 (enterprise request), SUP-18477 (latency regression), SUP-18506 (Private pinning + checksums).
- Engineering epic: ENG-4821 (Runtime LTS initiative) and related sub-tickets.

Appendix: strawman customer-facing language (very rough)
“Redwood Runtime LTS provides a stability-focused runtime baseline supported for 12 months with monthly patch updates and out-of-band security fixes. LTS patches include only security and critical reliability/performance fixes and are verified by extended test and performance gates. Customers can pin to a specific LTS patch in Dedicated and Private deployments, with signed artifacts and checksums for audit and rollback.”
